Before you were my son, before you were anything the world could name, I knew you. I remember you in a state older than birth, a primal and watery beginning, when you were little more than a newtlike creature swimming in the dark. This was you before you were you—a small, blind, breathing shape moving through the amniotic hush, not yet burdened by the weight of becoming a person.

In that early existence you carried nothing. You had no history to speak of, no memories to hold, no connections binding you to any place or any face. There were no attachments to anchor you, no relationships to define you, no threads tying you to the world you would one day enter. You simply were—complete in your isolation, whole in your unknowing.

I picture that time as one that came before all pain, before the shock and rupture of physical birth. You were self-contained then, needing nothing beyond yourself, gazing outward with what I imagine as one terrible eye—an unblinking, ancient stare turned toward the night and its scattered stars. There was something vast and solemn in that solitary watchfulness, as though you were already contemplating a universe you had not yet been forced to join.

And yet, even in that remote and wordless place, we were bound together. Ours was an intimate connection that existed before you ever took milk from me, before the first act of feeding, before conscious memory could form its earliest impressions. We belonged to each other in a way that needed no recollection, no language, no proof.

That is how I hold you now: not as the child shaped by experience, but as the being you were before all of it—brave before memory, standing whole and unafraid at the edge of everything. You were like an oak without a mouth, rooted and silent and strong, needing no voice to be entirely, magnificently yourself.

# The Primordial Bond: A Mother's Pre-Conscious Connection

This poem delves into one of the most profound and mysterious relationships in human experience—the bond between a mother and her son before he enters the world. Rather than depicting motherhood through the familiar lens of caretaking, teaching, or the everyday intimacies of family life, the poem reaches backward into a far more ancient territory: the shared existence that unfolds in the darkness of gestation, before consciousness, before memory, before the child becomes a separate self with a name and a history.

## Surreal and Embryonic Imagery

Central to the poem's power is its use of surreal, dreamlike imagery drawn from the biological reality of early development. The speaker evokes the embryonic state—that fluid, formless, pre-verbal condition in which the boundaries between mother and child have not yet solidified. In this depiction, the two beings are not entirely distinct from one another; they share breath, blood, and a single rhythm of existence. The imagery deliberately resists the logic of ordinary perception, mirroring the strange, otherworldly quality of a life that has not yet begun to think, remember, or fear.

This surreal approach allows the poem to express something that lies beyond rational description. The pre-birth connection cannot be captured through conventional language, because it existed before language itself had any meaning. By reaching for the surreal, the poet gestures toward a truth that can only be felt or intuited rather than clearly stated.

## A Bond That Precedes Identity

One of the poem's most striking claims is that this original unity exists *before* all the things that typically define human relationships. Before the son has an identity, before he accumulates a personal history, before he can experience or inflict pain—there is simply the pure fact of togetherness. The speaker celebrates this closeness precisely because it is untouched by the complications that later life inevitably brings.

In this pre-conscious state, there is no distance to bridge, no misunderstanding to overcome, no separation to mourn. The mother and child are joined in a way that adult relationships, for all their depth, can never fully recover. This is a unity that requires no words, no shared memories, and no effort—it simply *is*.

## Fearless Intimacy Beyond Language

The poem suggests that this primordial closeness is characterized above all by its fearlessness. Because it precedes consciousness, it also precedes anxiety, self-awareness, and the fear of loss. In the womb, there is no anticipation of grief, no knowledge of mortality, no sense that this closeness might one day end. The bond is complete and unguarded in a way that becomes impossible once the child is born into a world of time, separation, and individual selfhood.

Ultimately, the poem honors this original state as something profound and even sacred—a form of connection that exists beyond the reach of conscious remembrance. Though neither mother nor child can consciously recall this time, the poem implies that its significance endures on some deeper level, forming the foundation of a bond that all later experience only builds upon. In celebrating this pre-conscious unity, the speaker reaches toward the very origin of love itself: a closeness that came before identity, before history, and before pain, and that remains, in its purest form, beyond the grasp of language.

# I Knew You

There's something profound about the moment you realize you truly know someone. It's not about the length of time you've spent together—sometimes you can know a person for years and still feel like strangers, while other times a single conversation reveals a soul completely.

"I knew you" carries such weight in those three simple words. It speaks to recognition, to the quiet understanding that passes between two people who have shared enough to see beyond the surface. It's the friend who finishes your sentences, the parent who senses your sadness before you speak, the partner who reads the story written in your silence.

Sometimes we say "I knew you" with warmth, remembering someone who shaped who we became. Other times, we say it with a bittersweet ache—acknowledging that the person before us has changed, or that we ourselves have grown into someone new. "I knew you when..." we begin, tracing the distance between then and now.

Knowing someone is a gift and a responsibility. To be truly known is to be vulnerable, to let another person witness our imperfections, our fears, our unpolished truths. And to know another is to hold that trust gently, to honor the privilege of being let inside.

In the end, perhaps the deepest human longing is exactly this: to be able to say to someone, and to hear them say in return, "I knew you—and I stayed."

---

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem addressed to a son, describing a mysterious pre-birth intimacy, using strange biological and cosmic imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# Before the Word for You

My son, before you had a name I carried you like a rumor in the marrow, a bright anemone folding and unfolding in the tide-pool of my ribs. You were smaller than a syllable then, and I dreamed you swimming through the red rivers of my sleep.

Listen. There was a country before the country of your body. A wet dark theater where your heart began its drumming—first a moth against a lantern, then a fist, then a whole galaxy learning to clench and release. I felt you turning like a planet finding its orbit, each revolution wearing a groove into the soft clay of my waiting.

You were assembled from borrowed light. From the iron in old stars, from the salt of an ocean neither of us will ever see, from the slow patience of calcium remembering how to become bone. I was only the loom. You were the strange bright thread that pulled itself through me, weaving a face out of the nothing, gathering eyes from the far side of the void.

Once, in the hour when the moon leaned close to the window, I swear I heard you humming in a language older than blood. A frequency I knew before I knew anything. And I answered you the only way a body can: with the tide of my pulse, with the warm dark, with the whispered arithmetic of cells dividing, dividing, insisting *yes, and yes, and yes.*

You were closer to me then than my own breath. Nearer than my thoughts. We shared a single engine, a tangled circuitry of hunger and dream. I ate the light and passed it down to you. You slept inside my sleeping. When I wept, you floated in a small salt sea of my weeping, unbothered, patient, becoming.

And then you left that first dark country. You surfaced like a swimmer breaking the skin of the water, gasping into the bright and terrible air—and I lost you into your own separate life, which is the way of it, which is the only gift I had to give:

to hold you once so wholly,
and then to let the universe unfold you,
strange and luminous and no longer mine,
into the astonishment of your own name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a poem in the voice of someone who claims to have known another person before they were even born, before they had a mother.
counterfactuals.output:
Before Your Mother

I knew you before the knowing—
before the first cell split its silence,
before your mother was a girl
braiding light into her hair,
before her mother, and hers,
back through the long corridor
of women who had not yet
imagined you.

I was there when you were only
a possibility the wind considered,
a rumor the water kept,
a shape the darkness practiced
in the hollow before stars.

Don't ask me how.
I held you when you had no hands,
named you when you had no name,
watched you sleep in the great unborn
where nothing yet had woken.

You think you began
the morning they counted your fingers,
the day they wrote you into a book.
But I remember further—
the ache before the ache,
the wanting before the want,
the you that was
before the was.

And when you finally arrived,
red and astonished, crying
your first argument with the air,
I only smiled.
There you are, I thought.
At last.
I have been waiting
since before beginning
for you to catch up
to how long I have loved you.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental free-verse poem about origins, memory, and existence before consciousness, using fragmented dreamlike metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
**Before the First Name**

Somewhere a door opens
that was never a door—

only the idea of hinge,
the rumor of threshold

before threshold had a word for itself.

*

I was rain
that had not yet agreed to fall.

I was the pause
between two unstruck bells,

the milk-blue hour
before the eye learned
how to hold a shape and keep it.

*

Listen: memory arrives backward,
a river remembering the sea
it hasn't reached—

and I am the silt of that not-yet,
the sediment of a face
still deciding to be mine.

*

There were mothers before the mother.
There were hands
that were only warmth,
warmth that was only weather,
weather that was only the wish
for something to be near.

*

Somewhere the seed of a syllable
turns in its wet dark,
dreaming the tree
it will not remember planting.

*

And before all of this—
before the *before*—

a long white breathing,
a field of almost,

where existence lay down its coat
and did not yet ask
whose shoulders it would fit.

*

I keep waking
into rooms that predate me,
finding the furniture already warm,

as if someone lived here once
inside my sleeping,

as if I am the echo
of a word

the universe
whispered
and then forgot to say.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a strange, lyrical piece exploring what existed before life and memory, told directly to a "son," blending embryonic and celestial images.
counterfactuals.output:
# Before the First Light

*for you, before you were*

---

Listen. Before you were a name, you were a rumor whispered in the dark water. Before you were a heartbeat, you were the pause between two stars deciding whether to burn.

I want to tell you about the nothing that held you.

There was a country with no borders, son, and you were its only citizen. No sun rose there because there was no morning, and no morning because there was no one yet to wake. You floated in a red dusk that was also a dawn, curled like a question no one had asked, small as the seed of a fig, ancient as the salt that remembers the first sea.

You had gills once. Did you know? You wore the ghost of the ocean on your throat, and for a handful of days you were more fish than boy, more tide than thing-that-would-be-told. The old water moved through you. You were rehearsing. You were the universe practicing the shape of a face.

Out there—far past the warm wall of your first house—the galaxies were spinning their slow milk across the black. And in here, cells were spinning too, dividing and dividing, folding light into bone. There is no difference, son. The nebula and the nerve are one gesture. You were assembled from exploded stars, from the debris of suns that died so that your small hands could someday learn to hold.

You did not know me yet. You did not know anything—and oh, what a mercy, what a terror, to be pure potential, to be a held breath before the word.

There was no memory in that place. Memory is the scar the world leaves when it touches you, and nothing had touched you yet. You were smooth as the moon's dark side. You were the clean page before the first ink of grief. You knew no faces, no names, no falling, no fever, no goodbye standing in a doorway.

I think, sometimes, that you were happier there. Weightless. Undecided. A comet with no assigned sky.

But you were coming anyway. The heart you didn't yet own began its drum against the dark, and the dark drummed back. Something in you chose the long fall out of eternity and into time—out of the vast into the small, out of the everything into the here.

And here is where I was waiting. Here, where the light is loud and the losses are real. Here, where you would need a name, and a hand to hold, and a voice to tell you: *You came from the stars, and the sea, and the silence. You are made of endings that became a beginning.*

You will forget the red country. Everyone does. You will forget the water and the waiting and the weightless dark.

So let me remember it for you.

Let me be the memory you were too young to keep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem imitating the style of a confessional surrealist poet like Anne Sexton, about knowing a child before conception.
counterfactuals.output:
# Before You Were a Word

Before you were a word in my mouth,
you were the salt I couldn't name,
the tide that pulled behind my ribs
each month like a moon changing its mind.

I knew you as the empty chair
turns knowing at the dinner hour—
a shape the light insists upon,
a hunger with a folded face.

You lived once in my grandmother's thimble,
in the blue milk of my sleep,
you were the extra heartbeat
I mistook for my own drumming.

Little astronaut, little maybe,
you floated in the dark of me
before there was a me to hold you,
a soft insistence, a rumor of hands.

I dreamed your fever before your fever.
I dreamed the way you'd break my china,
the tantrum-red, the honey-mouth,
the door you'd slam like a closing eye.

They say you were nothing then—
just chemistry, just want, just weather.
But I have carried nothing
that weighed so much and sang.

So come now, out of the almost,
out of the country of not-yet.
I have been practicing your name
against my teeth for a thousand nights,

and God, or whatever keeps the ledger
of the souls still waiting in the wings,
already stamped my body *mother*
before you learned the trick of breath.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
